title: A crash-safe embedded key-value store whose durability is observed rather than asserted
description: An embedded key-value store with a write-ahead log. Durability is observed by a simulated disk with a durable and a pending layer, for both file contents and directory entries: Sync and syncDir promote, Crash discards, and a test puts, cuts the power, reopens and requires the value. Deleting the log fsync, either checkpoint directory sync, or the torn-tail truncation each turns the suite red. A 240-seed randomised crash corpus runs alongside it in CI and covers different ground - it cannot detect a missing fsync at all, because a process kill leaves the page cache intact.

clauses.text: A write the store has acknowledged is present after a crash immediately following that acknowledgement. A write not yet acknowledged may be absent, and that is not a failure.
clauses.observable_by: the crash harness records the set of acknowledged keys before each kill and asserts every one is readable after recovery, while the single in-flight unacknowledged key is permitted to be absent, unchanged or applied
clauses.rationale: This distinction is the entire contract of a durable store. Losing an unacknowledged write is correct behaviour; losing an acknowledged one is data loss. A suite that does not encode the difference is not testing durability, it is testing that the happy path works twice.

clauses.text: Durability comes from fsync, not from write returning. No acknowledgement is issued before the log's fsync returns, and creating the log file fsyncs the directory that contains it.
clauses.observable_by: the store writes through a simulated file with a durable layer and a pending layer, where only Sync promotes pending to durable; a test acknowledges a write, takes the power away, reopens and requires the value to be there - so a commit path with the fsync removed loses the data and the test fails. The event-ordering test (sync-start, sync-return, ack) is kept alongside it as a check on the sequence, but it is self-report and nothing rests on it. On a platform with directory fsync the sync of the containing directory is asserted at log creation, and on a platform without it the test asserts the store reports the guarantee as unavailable rather than claiming it
clauses.rationale: A successful write(2) guarantees nothing - the bytes sit in the page cache and a power cut loses them. The directory entry for a newly created file needs its own fsync or the file itself can vanish. This is the most common thing people get wrong.

clauses.text: Every log record carries a checksum over its own bytes and a sequence number linking it to the previous one. A record failing either check ends recovery at that point and is never returned as data.
clauses.observable_by: tests that flip a byte inside a record, truncate a record mid-write, and break the sequence chain each assert that recovery stops cleanly at the last intact record and that no value written after the damage is ever returned from Get
clauses.rationale: A page is not written atomically by the OS. A crash mid-write leaves a torn record, and a store that trusts it returns garbage that surfaces as a bug somewhere unrelated. Per-record checksums plus a sequence chain make a torn tail detectable rather than silently plausible.

clauses.text: Recovery is deterministic. The same log replayed twice produces byte-identical state.
clauses.observable_by: recovery run twice over the same directory produces an identical serialised snapshot compared byte for byte, over hand-built logs and over every log left behind by the randomised crash corpus
clauses.rationale: Non-deterministic recovery means a crash can leave two machines reading the same log and disagreeing about the data. It also makes every other durability test unfalsifiable, because a failure cannot be reproduced.

clauses.text: Crash injection at randomised points never corrupts the store, and the harness is genuinely randomised with a recorded seed rather than a handful of hand-placed crash points.
clauses.observable_by: the harness forks a child that writes under a seeded schedule, kills it at a randomised offset, reopens in the parent and asserts B1, B3 and B4; the seed is printed on every run, the spread of kill points across the corpus is asserted to be non-degenerate, a failing seed reproduces the same failure with one documented command, and a deliberately unsynced build is caught by the same harness
clauses.rationale: This is the headline clause and the one a sceptical reader checks first. Hand-placed crash points prove almost nothing - they test the paths the author already thought about, which are exactly the paths that are already correct.

clauses.text: The write-ahead log is bounded. Checkpointing runs, and the log does not grow without limit under sustained writes.
clauses.observable_by: a sustained-write test asserts live log segment bytes stay under a stated bound while total bytes written exceeds that bound by at least an order of magnitude, and that acknowledged writes still survive a crash taken during and after checkpointing
clauses.rationale: An unbounded log works in a demo and fills the disk in production. Checkpointing is also where crash-safety bugs concentrate, because it is the one path that deletes data on purpose.

cases.description: a flipped byte inside a record is caught by the checksum; recovery stops at the previous record
a record truncated mid-write is discarded, not half-applied
a broken sequence chain stops recovery rather than skipping the gap

a characterisation case, and the only one in this contract that records a limitation rather than a guarantee. The checksum chain restarts at zero at each segment boundary because a checkpoint may have deleted the segment the first record would otherwise chain to, so a whole segment taken from a different store and dropped in at a matching base is accepted and recovery serves the other store crash-safely and wrongly. A guard, not a probe, because there is no implementation it catches - it pins behaviour so the README cannot overstate the chaining again, and it names the line to rewrite if the boundary is ever closed. crc32c is a checksum, not a MAC: this is a crash model, not a threat model

a garbage length prefix is treated as end of log. Three lengths: one past the ceiling, most of a uint32, and the high bit set. The last two are arch-sensitive and were failing under GOARCH=386 from the day the test was written until 29145d4 - int is 32 bits there, so converting the on-disk uint32 before bounding it made the length negative and the slice bound after it negative too, which panics inside recovery. The description this case used to carry said the ceiling stops an allocation, and there is no allocation on this path

a length past the ceiling, inside a buffer that is genuinely long enough to hold it. Every other length case in this unit is rejected because the buffer is too short, which is what a torn tail looks like and is not what a merely corrupt length looks like: with the ceiling deleted those cases stay green and this one does not. It is the case that makes the ceiling load-bearing on a 64-bit build rather than decorative
the bytes are on disk the instant Put returns: replaying the log file alone, with no in-memory state and no Close, yields the key
a write whose record was torn by the crash is permitted to be absent, and its absence is not reported as an error - asserts the suite does not over-claim
the recorded event order is sync-start, sync-return, ack - never ack before sync-return

the store always reaches the directory-sync decision when a log segment is created, and what it reports about itself matches the build it is - claiming the guarantee where it has it and reporting it unavailable where it does not. This case is about honest self-report and nothing else; that the sync actually makes the entry durable is simulated-disk/new-segments-directory-entry-is-made-durable, because an emitted event cannot establish it
two replays of one directory serialise to identical bytes
two stores with the same final contents written in different orders serialise identically

a directory holding a segment based at 0 and a segment based at 20 with the one based at 10 missing: recovery must stop at the hole and serve the records before it, never the records past it. Every segment starts its own checksum chain, so nothing inside the later segment is detectably wrong - the only evidence the missing records existed is that the second segment does not begin where the first one ended. This is the premise docs/verification.md leans on to downgrade the superseded-record skip, and it was untested until now

the oldest surviving segment begins after the sequence the checkpoint covers, so records in between are in neither file and no later comparison can detect it. Open must return an error rather than a store that is quietly missing writes
live log segment bytes stay under the stated bound while total bytes written exceeds it by 10x or more
acknowledged writes survive reopening after a checkpoint, including writes made before the checkpoint

a checkpoint at sequence 30 over a superseded segment holding records 1..15 and then a record that never finished. Replay stops inside the superseded range, so what it has applied is a PREFIX of records the checkpoint already covers, and a prefix puts stale values back over newer ones. Deleting the skip in loadDir turns this red on all ten keys and on the snapshot comparison - on data, not on the report field that was previously the only thing standing between this store and silent re-application. The directory is hand-built: it needs a torn tail in a segment that is not the last one, which the store does not currently produce, so this pins recovery against a log the FORMAT admits rather than a crash the store can take. The neighbouring window - every superseded record surviving - is idempotent and CANNOT fail on data, which is stated in both tests

the second characterisation case in this contract, and the measurement behind a premise the documentation argues from. checkpointLocked unlinks superseded segments oldest first, so a crash part way through leaves a suffix; two separate arguments here lean on that and neither had been measured against the alternative. Leave a prefix instead - the oldest segment still under a checkpoint that covers it, the live segment above the hole - and recovery stops at the hole and OpenWith then deletes everything past it: ten acknowledged records gone, no crash involved. A guard rather than a probe because it records what happens today rather than requiring it. Closing the gap means loadDir refusing to open when the stop is a gap between segments rather than a torn tail at the end, which changes when the store declines to open and has the 240-seed corpus downstream
a checkpoint file left half-written by a crash is rejected by its checksum and recovery falls back to the log

units.note: The store writes through a simulated file whose bytes only become durable when Sync is called, so a power cut can be staged in-process. This is the only place in the repository where a missing fsync is detectable: after Process.Kill the page cache is intact, so the crash corpus cannot see one.

cases.description: writes are acknowledged, the simulated power is cut with no Close, and a second store opened on the same platter returns every one of them - the assertion is on the data, not on any event or counter the store reports about itself

a newly created log segment is deleted by the simulated power cut unless the store has synced the containing directory, so removing fsys.syncDir() from createSegment loses the whole log. This proves the store PERFORMS the directory sync at the point it has to; whether the platform's implementation of that call makes the entry durable is a claim about the platform, made in syncdir_unix.go and syncdir_windows.go and not by this test
the same, driven past the checkpoint bound, so the checkpoint's own fsync and the ordering around it are covered too

an fsync is interrupted 30 bytes into a record, leaving a torn tail produced by the real write path rather than spliced in by the test; every acknowledged write before it is recoverable, the partial record is not returned, and - the half nothing else covered - the reopened log is cut back to the last vouched-for byte, so a write acknowledged after recovery is still readable after the next power cut

the deliberately broken kvearlyack build is required to FAIL the power-cut test, and to fail it by losing an acknowledged key rather than for any other reason. Deterministic on every platform, which the process-kill negative control is not: the same broken build and the same 24 seeds were caught 13 times on windows/amd64 and 4 times on ubuntu-latest

the power is taken out at the create immediately after the rename that installs a checkpoint, and the checkpoint has to be on the platter. rename(2) is atomic with respect to a reader, which is not the same as durable: until the directory is fsynced a reopening process still finds the old name. Deleting fsys.syncDir() after the rename in writeCheckpoint turns this red with recovery finding no checkpoint at all. Nothing is LOST either way - the ordering in checkpointLocked reverts the checkpoint and the deletions together and the test asserts that too - so what this pins is that the store having said it installed a checkpoint is true one instruction later

an unlink is a directory write, so until the directory is synced the entry comes back and with it the log the checkpoint had just superseded. Deleting s.fsys.syncDir() at the end of checkpointLocked turns this red, naming the segment that reappeared. Before the simulated disk staged metadata this deletion left all 28 root tests green

an fsync that returns EIO has still returned, and the write it covered is not on the platter. This was red when written and found a real defect rather than a staged one: after a commit failed part way, w.wrote had moved past bytes the log could not vouch for, so the NEXT record was written beyond the point recovery stops at - fsynced, acknowledged and unreachable. The assertion is the contract itself, not the symptom: every key whose Put returned nil must be readable after the power cut
a WriteAt that takes ten bytes of a two-hundred-byte record and stops. Same defect, same red, same fix: the segment refuses every later write rather than chaining on top of a partial record

a WriteAt that takes no bytes at all. Declared a guard rather than a probe because it was green when written and I could not produce an honest implementation that it catches and the two cases above do not - nothing reached the file, so there is no gap to write past. It is here because a caller cannot tell how far a failed write got, so the guarantee must not depend on it

a ReadAt that fails during replay must not be mistaken for the end of the log, or Open returns a store silently missing every record after the bad sector. Red proof: changing readErr = err to _ = err at file.go:173 turns it red reporting 0 applied records and 0 live keys - and left the whole suite green before this case existed

file.go documents that create fails on an existing name and that checkpointLocked relies on it to catch a segment it would otherwise silently reopen and write over from the start. Red proof: removing os.O_EXCL from osFS.create turns it red, and left the whole suite green before this case existed

a later page of a write is made durable while an earlier page of the same write is not, leaving a hole; recovery stops at the hole and never scans forward to the intact tail sitting beyond it. Declared a guard rather than a probe because it has no honest red proof: this store never had a scanning recovery to break, so there is no implementation of it that this case catches and record_test.go does not. Its value is that the shape is produced by the real write path and is one the crash corpus was measured to produce zero of.

a segment that refused writes after a commit failed has to come back. Reopening replays every record acknowledged before the failure, returns nothing the failed Puts wrote, leaves the segment holding exactly the bytes recovery vouched for, and takes a new write that survives the next power cut. Red proof: deleting the f.Truncate(validBytes) in reopenSegment turns it red on the length assertion, and that deletion left the whole suite green before this case existed - root package and 240-seed corpus both

a short write poisons the live segment, and the caller then makes the exported Checkpoint() call the doc comment invites. checkpointLocked wrote the checkpoint, created the successor, moved s.log to it and only THEN got the stored failure back from closing the old segment - so it returned before unlinking anything, leaving a segment with a tail recovery cannot vouch for underneath a store now acknowledging writes into its successor. The next Open stops at that tail and DELETES the successor. Two acknowledged writes gone on a healthy machine with no crash, no torn page and no power cut anywhere in the sequence, and unrecoverable by hand afterwards because the successor is unlinked and the directory synced. The assertion is on the data: Checkpoint returns an error either way, because closing a failed segment reports the failure whether or not it was allowed to rotate first

the power goes at the end of each of the ten filesystem calls the checkpoint path makes, one run per call, and every acknowledged key is still readable afterwards. This is the premise the removal of the directory sync before the checkpoint rename rests on: nothing is unlinked until the checkpoint that supersedes it is durable. It does NOT decide one directory sync against two - both pass, because the only difference is a stray CHECKPOINT.tmp no reader consults, and that is recorded as a gap rather than papered over. Red proof: unlinking the superseded segments before writeCheckpoint instead of after turns five of the ten crash points red, naming the keys that went

units.note: Two knobs, because they are two questions. Whether the store's syncDir does anything is the PLATFORM's code - a real fsync(2) in syncdir_unix.go, a no-op in syncdir_windows.go. Whether the directory is journalled is the FILESYSTEM's behaviour - ext4 data=ordered against NTFS $LogFile. The Windows build is the first paired with the second, and nothing in simdisk_test.go could express that pairing before. What this unit proves is the store being correct GIVEN the documented NTFS contract; whether NTFS honours that contract is not reachable by any model here, and docs/verification.md files that residual rather than closing it.

cases.description: under the NTFS rule - metadata journalled, so a create is durable as it is issued - a no-op syncDir still leaves an acknowledged write recoverable across a power cut. This is the Windows pairing, and it is the case that says syncdir_windows.go's twenty-line argument is correct rather than merely written down

the control, and a guard rather than a probe because it passes from the first commit on purpose and there is no implementation bug it catches. The same no-op syncDir against the POSIX rule LOSES the acknowledged write, which is why syncdir_unix.go exists. Without it the journalled assertion above would be vacuous in a way no red proof could reveal: it could pass against a simulated disk that had quietly stopped modelling directory entries at all, which is the same trap TestANewSegmentsDirectoryEntryIsMadeDurable guards with its orphan preamble
the recorded seed corpus runs end to end with zero acknowledged writes lost and zero corrupt reads
the corpus kills children at a spread of different points, not the same one every time - a degenerate spread would make the corpus size meaningless
a deliberately unsynced build fails under the harness, prints its seed, and that seed reproduces the identical failure while the honest build passes it
the recorded corpus is at least 200 seeds and the count is printed

replaying one preserved crash directory five times produces the identical findings in the identical order, compared verbatim rather than by category and count. The previous test compared sorted Kinds() and len(Failures), which is shaped around the map-order defect instead of catching it

the shape tally prints a row for every shape the classifier can produce, zeros included, and the enumerated set cannot drift away from the classifier. The README leans on three zero rows and the command that is offered as the check could not emit one

a run that goes short names the seeds it never reached rather than reporting a count of them. "9 never attempted" tells a reader the corpus was short and gives them nothing to re-run, which is the one thing the whole seeded design is for. Red proof: the first version of the tally computed the shortfall as corpus minus observations minus attempts and had no seed identities to print

two observations of seed 11 and none of seed 22 is two observations over a corpus of two: the arithmetic balances and a count-based reconciliation reports a complete corpus while one seed stood in for another. Red proof: the first version compared totals, and this reconciled green

an observation recorded for a seed that is not in the corpus being reconciled against means the thing feeding the tally and the thing checking it disagree about what is being run, and the totals can still balance while it happens. Red proof: the first version compared totals and reconciled green over it

Tally's doc comment claims the count and the verdict come out of the same call, so a caller cannot print the reassuring half without being handed the other half. That is a claim about the API surface and one exported method returning a bare count falsifies it. Red proof: Observations() int existed and this named it. What the case does NOT establish: that a caller prints both halves - only that it was told both

the link between the tally and the corpus: given a reconciliation that does not add up, the corpus test fails and the failure names the seeds that went unrun; given one that does, it logs the line on the green path too, because a number that only appears when something went wrong is not evidence that anything went right. A guard rather than a probe because the behaviour was written inline in TestSeededCorpusNoAckedLoss and already held - extracting it made it reachable, it catches no implementation that ever shipped. It was checked in both directions: deleting the failure branch turns it red naming the short run. What it does NOT establish is that t.Errorf inside t.Cleanup fails the package, which is the standard library's guarantee and is not re-proven here
every directory left behind by the corpus replays to byte-identical state twice

the README's opening sentence claims 240 seeds; CorpusFloor is 200 and the generator comparison is prefix-only, so forty could be trimmed with every gate still green while the first thing a reader sees became false. Separate from corpus-size-floor on purpose: the floor says the corpus is large enough to be evidence, this says it is the size the front page claims

non_goals: Concurrency beyond a single process holding the directory. There is no MVCC, no reader snapshot isolation and no multi-process access.
Range scans, iterators, transactions or a secondary index. This is a durability demonstration, not a database.
Competing with a real storage engine on throughput. Every write costs an fsync by default and that is the point.
Proving the guarantee against real power loss. Nothing in userspace can do that; the harness proves the process can die at any instruction, not that the drive honours its flush.
open_questions: Directory fsync has no Windows equivalent. The store reports it as unavailable there rather than claiming it - is reporting enough, or should Open refuse to run in a mode it cannot back?
